agent_spawn.agent.description: Launch a sub-agent to work on a task.
agent_spawn.agent.tool_prompt:
Spawns an isolated sub-agent to work on a task.

## How to use
- By default (wait=true): blocks until the agent finishes and returns its result
- With wait=false: launches the agent in background, returns an agent_id
- For parallel work: call Agent multiple times in the same turn — they run concurrently
- Each agent has its own context — include all needed information in prompt
- The agent shares your workspace, filesystem, and memory

## Tips
- Make prompts self-contained — the agent cannot see your conversation
- Use specialist='explore' for codebase search, 'plan' for architecture
- For background agents, use AgentWaitAll later to collect results

## Example — parallel research
Call all 3 in the same turn:
  Agent(prompt='Find all API endpoints in src/api/', description='API endpoints')
  Agent(prompt='List all database models', description='DB models')
  Agent(prompt='Check test coverage', description='Test coverage')

## Example — background
  Agent(prompt='Run full test suite', description='Running tests', wait=false)
  ... continue working ...
  AgentWaitAll()  # collect results when ready

    description: string (optional) -- Short label shown in the UI (e.g. 'Search for login usages').
    specialist: string (optional) -- Agent type: 'explore', 'plan', 'worker', 'verification'. Omit for general.
    wait: boolean (optional) -- Wait for the agent to finish and return its result. Set false to run in background.

context_builder.ask_user.description: Ask the user a question and WAIT for their response. The agent pauses until the user replies. Supports: simple questions, multiple choices, content review, and structured forms.
context_builder.ask_user.tool_prompt:
Ask the user a question and WAIT for their response.
The agent pauses completely until the user replies — use this wisely.

## When to use
- Before destructive actions (delete, overwrite)
- When choosing between approaches
- To review a plan or code before proceeding
- When you need specific information the user hasn't provided

## Modes

**Simple question** — just ask:
  ask_user(question="Should I proceed with this plan?")

**With choices** — user clicks a button instead of typing:
  ask_user(question="Which framework?", choices=["FastAPI", "Django", "Flask"])

**Multi-select choices:**
  ask_user(question="Which features?", choices=["Auth", "DB", "Tests", "Docker"], allow_multiple=true)

**Content review** — user sees and can edit a long document:
  ask_user(question="Review and approve this plan.", content="## Plan\n1. Create auth\n2. Add routes\n3. Write tests")

**Structured form** — user fills in multiple fields:
  ask_user(question="Configure the project", form=[
    {"type": "select", "name": "framework", "label": "Framework", "options": ["FastAPI", "Django"]},
    {"type": "text", "name": "name", "label": "Project name", "placeholder": "my-app"},
    {"type": "checkbox", "name": "features", "label": "Features", "options": ["Auth", "DB", "Tests"]},
    {"type": "toggle", "name": "docker", "label": "Docker?", "default": true}
  ])

## Form field types
- select: dropdown with options
- text: single line input
- textarea: multi-line input
- checkbox: multiple select with checkboxes
- toggle: on/off switch
- number: numeric input

## Rules
- Do NOT ask trivial questions — use your best judgment for simple decisions
- Do NOT ask multiple questions in one call — split them
- If the user already gave you enough info, just proceed
- Use choices when there are 2-6 clear options
- Use form when you need multiple pieces of info at once
- Use content when presenting a plan or code for review

database.sql.description: Execute a SQL query and return results.
database.sql.tool_prompt:
Execute SQL on the configured database and return results.

## Query types
- SELECT: returns rows as a list of objects
- INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE: returns affected row count
- CREATE/ALTER/DROP: returns success status

## Tips
- Use parameterized queries for safety: query='SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?', params=[42]
- NEVER use string interpolation for user input — always use params
- Use LIMIT to avoid returning too many rows

query: string (required) -- Any SQL query. SELECT returns rows, DML returns affected count. Always add LIMIT to SELECT.
    params: array (optional) -- Positional parameters for :p0, :p1, :p2 placeholders. Example: ['alice@example.com', 42]
    connection_id: string (optional) -- Connection to use. Default: 'default'

schema.description:
Execute any SQL query — the UNIVERSAL database action.

Auto-detects query type:
- SELECT / WITH / SHOW / EXPLAIN → returns rows as a list of dicts
- INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE → returns affected row count
- CREATE / ALTER / DROP → returns success confirmation

This single action replaces: execute_query, fetch_results, batch_execute,
bulk_insert, explain_query, browse, search_data.

Tips:
- Always add LIMIT to SELECT queries to avoid huge results (default cap: 100 rows)
- Use EXPLAIN before complex queries to check performance
- Use parameterized queries for user input: sql(query="SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = :p0", params=[42])
- For bulk inserts, write standard INSERT statements with VALUES
- For transactions: BEGIN; INSERT ...; INSERT ...; COMMIT; (in separate sql calls)

Examples:
    sql(query="SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 10")
    sql(query="SELECT name, email FROM users WHERE active = true ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20")
    sql(query="SELECT u.name, count(o.id) as order_count FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id GROUP BY u.name ORDER BY order_count DESC LIMIT 10")
    sql(query="INSERT INTO users (name, email) VALUES ('Alice', 'alice@example.com')")
    sql(query="UPDATE users SET active = false WHERE last_login < '2024-01-01'")
    sql(query="DELETE FROM sessions WHERE expired_at < datetime('now')")
    sql(query="CREATE TABLE logs (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, message TEXT, created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP)")
    sql(query="EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42")
    sql(query="SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = :p0", params=["alice@example.com"])
    sql(query="SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'pending'", connection_id="analytics")

query.description: Any SQL query. SELECT returns rows, DML returns affected count. Always add LIMIT to SELECT.
query.title: Query

filesystem.edit.description: Perform exact string replacements in a file.
filesystem.edit.tool_prompt:
Performs exact string replacements in files. This is your primary tool for modifying existing code.

## How to use Edit correctly
1. FIRST use Read to see the file content (required for files > 500 bytes)
2. COPY the exact text you want to change from the Read output as old_string
3. Write the replacement as new_string (same indentation level)
4. Check the 'lint' field in the result — fix any errors immediately

## Rules
- old_string must be COPIED from Read output — never type it from memory
- Include 1-2 surrounding lines for uniqueness (e.g. the function signature above the line you're changing)
- Preserve exact indentation (tabs/spaces) as shown in Read output
- Do NOT include line numbers from Read output in old_string or new_string
- Keep changes minimal — replace only what needs to change
- Use replace_all=true only for renaming a variable/function across the whole file
- new_string can be empty to delete the matched text

## Example
If Read shows:
  10| def greet(name):
  11|     return f"hello {name}"

To change the return value, call Edit with:
  path: "src/utils.py"
  old_string: "def greet(name):\n    return f\"hello {name}\""
  new_string: "def greet(name):\n    return f\"hi {name}!\""

## If Edit fails
- 'old_string not found': Re-read the file, the content may have changed. Copy the exact text again.
- 'old_string appears N times': Add more surrounding lines to old_string to make it unique.
- 'You have not read the file': Call Read first, then retry the Edit.

file_path: string (required) -- The absolute path to the file to modify.
    old_string: string (required) -- The text to replace. Copy this from Read output. Must be unique in the file.
    new_string: string (required) -- The text to replace it with. Must be different from old_string.
    replace_all: boolean (optional) -- Replace all occurrences of old_string. Default: false.

Searches file contents using regex patterns. Built on ripgrep.

## When to use
- Find where a function/class/variable is defined or used
- Search before Read — find the exact file and line number first
- NEVER use Bash with grep/rg — always use this tool instead

## Tips
- Supports full regex: 'log.*Error', 'function\s+\w+', 'import.*json'
- Filter by file type with include: '*.py', '*.{ts,tsx}'
- Use context parameter to see surrounding lines (e.g. context=3)
- Literal braces need escaping: 'interface\{\}' to find 'interface{}'
- For cross-line patterns, use multiline mode

## Workflow: Grep → Read → Edit
1. Grep to find where the code is (file + line number)
2. Read to see the exact content around that area
3. Edit to make the change (copy old_string from Read output)

Reads a file and returns its content with line numbers. You can access any file directly.

shell.bash.tool_prompt:
Executes a shell command and returns stdout, stderr, and exit code.

## When to use Bash
- git commands, build tools, test runners, package managers, system commands
- Do NOT use Bash when a dedicated tool exists:
  - Read files: use Read (NOT cat/head/tail)
  - Edit files: use Edit (NOT sed/awk)
  - Create files: use Write (NOT echo/cat)
  - Search content: use Grep (NOT grep/rg)
  - Find files: use Glob (NOT find/ls)

## Background mode
- For long-running commands (servers, builds, large test suites): set run_in_background=true
- Returns a task_id — use BashStatus(task_id=...) to check progress or get results

## Tips
- Chain commands with && (sequential) or ; (independent)
- Quote file paths with spaces using double quotes
- The working directory persists between calls
- Git safety: never skip hooks (--no-verify), never force push, always create NEW commits

command: string (required) -- Shell command to execute. Use && to chain commands, ; for independent commands.
    description: string (optional) -- Short label shown in the UI (e.g. 'Running tests').

## BackgroundRun
Launch any tool as a background task.
Run a tool in the background — returns a task_id immediately.

## When to use
- Long-running operations: downloads, database migrations, large file processing
- Any tool call that might take more than a few seconds
- Use BackgroundStatus(task_id=...) to check progress and get results

## Format
- By tool name: BackgroundRun(name='database.sql', params={query: 'SELECT ...'})
- By shell command: BackgroundRun(command='npm run build')
Parameters:
    name: string (optional) -- Fully qualified tool name (module.action).
    params: object (optional) -- Parameters for the action.
    command: string (optional) -- Shell command (auto-routes to shell.background_run).
    cwd: string (optional) -- Working directory (shell shortcut).
    env: object (optional) -- Environment variables (shell shortcut).

## BackgroundStatus
Check the status and result of a background task.
Check on a background task launched with BackgroundRun.

## Returns
- If running: status, elapsed time
- If completed: status, full result, elapsed time
- If failed: status, error message, elapsed time
Parameters:
    task_id: string (required) -- Task ID returned by background_run.

## Sql
Execute a SQL query and return results.
Execute SQL on the configured database and return results.

## Query types
- SELECT: returns rows as a list of objects
- INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE: returns affected row count
- CREATE/ALTER/DROP: returns success status

## Tips
- Use parameterized queries for safety: query='SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?', params=[42]
- NEVER use string interpolation for user input — always use params
- Use LIMIT to avoid returning too many rows
Parameters:
    query: string (required) -- Any SQL query. SELECT returns rows, DML returns affected count. Always add LIMIT to SELECT.
    params: array (optional) -- Positional parameters for :p0, :p1, :p2 placeholders. Example: ['alice@example.com', 42]
    connection_id: string (optional) -- Connection to use. Default: 'default'
